newsitem.title: USA: South Africa's Mbeki discusses Zaire in Washington.
newsitem.headline: South Africa's Mbeki discusses Zaire in Washington.

text.p: South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki said on Thursday he hoped Zairean peace talks would resume early next week and there is not a plan for embattled Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko to leave power.
He spoke briefly with reporters at the State Department after talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
Earlier, on arrival in Washington, he told South African Broadcasting that "I don't think we would respond negatively" to a request from Mobutu to seek asylum in South Africa.
But Mbeki said there has been no suggestion so far that Mobutu would want to seek asylum.
Mbeki convened the Zaire peace talks along with Mohamed Sahnoun, representative of the United Nations and the Organization of African Unity.
Zaire's warring sides ended four days of peace talks in South Africa on Tuesday and said they agreed on the need for a ceasefire and democratic elections.
Delegates representing Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who met for the first time in Pretoria on Saturday, then left for consultations with their leaders.

Mbeki said he briefed Albright on the talks. "We are all pursuing a negotiated resolution of this matter, a cessation of hostilities. We are all pulling in the same direction with regard to those issues," he said.

Asked if there was a concrete scenario for Mobutu leaving power, he replied: "No. The whole matter of what happens to the governance of Zaire is something that is on the agenda of the negotiations ... and I'm sure that wil be included, the future of Mobutu."
"So it's not a matter that can be decided outside of that process of negotiation," he added.
As for the peace talks, "we're hoping we can resume the beginning of next week," Mbeki said.
The United States signalled on Wednesday that Mobutu should step down, effectively ending a decades-old alliance with the African strongman.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said a negotiated solution to Zaire's civil war, which Washington has been pressing for, must include agreements on interim transitional government arrangements leading ultimately to elections.

The United States is braced for a possible evacuation of about 450 Americans from the country. Some 1,400 U.S. Marines were stationed offshore in case the call to evacuate was made. Officials said the situation was being watched closely.
Kabila's rebels Thursday tightened the screws on Mobutu, consolidating their hold on its economic heart and giving him three days to start talks on quitting.
Rebels forces ended the battle for the nation's southern second city Lubumbashi, driving Mobutu loyalists from its airport and sending them fleeing into the bush.
